abstract_summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are evolving from single-session tools toward long-term personal assistants that must adapt to individual users across tasks, contexts, and interactions. This shift makes memory a core requirement for personalization, since user preferences, goals, constraints, relationships, and pa...

representations can model not only what an agent remembers
about a user but also how memories are connected, revised, and

work remains fragmented across personalized agents and generic
graph memory frameworks, making it difficult to understand the
design space as a whole. This survey develops a lifecycle-oriented
view of graph-based personalized memory for LLM agents. We
organize existing studies around memory representation, memory
evolution, memory retrieval, and memory evaluation. We further

and open challenges in building reliable long-term personalized

support adaptive, controllable, and user-centric LLM agents. The

Our contributions are as follows:
•Taxonomy. We develop a lifecycle taxonomy that or-
ganizes existing studies on graph-based personalized
memory around representation, evolution, retrieval, and
evaluation.
•Evaluation. We summarize existing benchmarks and
metrics and identify gaps in graph quality, user control,
lifecycle validity, and realistic personalization.
•Timely Review. For each category, we review recent
methods and discuss their motivations, graph structures,
and user-modeling functions.
•Future Directions. We outline several open research
directions to guide future research on this promising
topic.
II. PRELIMINARIES
A. Graph-based Personalized Memory
Personalization refers to an LLM agent adapting its re-
sponses, retrieval, and actions to an individual user.

prior states, consolidate accumulated memory, and remove
outdated records. This section examines these five evolution
operations (illustrated in Fig. 3).
A. Memory Admission
Admission decides whether incoming evidence becomes
persistent memory and at what functional type or granularity.
In KGT [35], user feedback is treated as a trigger to add or re-
place factual triples in its graph. MemORAI [21] applies selec-
tive filtering and compression to retain user-persona-relevant
episodic content, facts, and preferences while compressing less
informative discourse. MemGuard [40] assigns each memory
a functional role (e.g., fact, procedural instruction, constraint)
at write time and preserves boundaries among functionally
distinct memory types. Admission protocol is important as
over-admission risks 
[… separate evidence block …]
embedding transient claims as durable
user state, while under-admission can discard evidence that
later interactions require.
B. Memory Integration
After admission, integration attaches evidence to the ex-
isting graph structure at a local write scale. Append-and-
link preserves provenance to the originating turn, session, or
chunk, as in LiCoMemory [10]. To reduce redundancy when
admitting memory, Mem0 g [31] reuses semantically matched
nodes and invalidates obsolete edges, while HingeMem [36]
consolidates near-duplicate boundary hyperedges. GAM [22]
uses buffered attachment, writing new utterances into an active
event graph before later consolidation into its global graph.
This ensures GAM only consolidates semantically complete
units and reduces semantic drift in the main graph.
C. Conflict Resolution
Conflict resolution addresses incoming evidence that
changes the validity or scope

Across these benchmarks, reported metrics fall into five
groups:
•Answer quality:F1, exact match, multiple-choice accu-

•Evidence retrieval:Recall@k, NDCG@k, answer-turn

•User-state modeling:preference-category accuracy, pro-
file or persona consistency, and correctness or helpfulness
of personalized responses.
•Memory evolution and structure:update success, step
or chain accuracy under changing environments, forget-
ting/update outcomes, structure-requiring task accuracy,
and failure-attribution

VII. CHALLENGES ANDFUTUREDIRECTIONS
Personalized graph memory remains a young but promising
research frontier. Its central challenge is not merely storing
user information in graph form but building a long-term,
trustworthy, and actionable model of an individual user, which
in turn motivates several future directions.

answers correctly, retrieves supporting evidence, verifies up-
dated user state, or reduces context cost over long histories.

positive_signals: The survey develops a lifecycle-oriented taxonomy organizing graph-based personalized memory for LLM agents around representation, evolution, retrieval, and evaluation.
The survey's contribution includes a taxonomy, an evaluation summary identifying gaps, a timely review of recent methods, and future directions.

The survey positions itself against prior surveys of personalized agents and graph-based agent memory, which use different primary lenses and do not provide a unified account of graph-based personalized memory.
The survey organizes representation into five patterns: flat, hierarchical, hypergraph, hybrid, and multiple disjoint graphs, and reviews systems within each pattern.
The survey identifies five evolution operations: admission, integration, conflict resolution, consolidation, and removal, and reviews systems implementing each.
The survey summarizes representative personalized-memory benchmarks and their evaluation metrics, organized into five metric groups.
The survey acknowledges that graph structure does not automatically improve retrieval, since controlled comparisons show results can depend on foundational system settings beyond graph structure.
The survey notes that the multiple disjoint graphs design is supported by limited evidence, and the cited work does not establish whether the graph instances are formally disjoint.
The survey maintains a continuously updated repository of surveyed works.
